name: ares
why: Automatically chains through encodings and ciphers to decode text, a fun puzzle-solving transform for exploring classical crypto.

brief.what_it_is: Ciphey is a command-line tool and Rust library that takes encoded or encrypted text and works out the chain of decoders needed to recover the plaintext, with no key, cipher name, or hint supplied. It searches through combinations of encodings and classical ciphers such as Base64, hex, Caesar/ROT13, Vigenere, and Morse, several layers deep. Input is text pasted or read from a file, and the output is the candidate plaintext, the decoder path used (for example Base64 → Hexadecimal → caesar), and any key it found. It runs under a time limit, five seconds by default.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as the next generation of Ciphey, a Python decoding tool that the same author plans to replace. The pitch is speed: Ciphey is 'very fast', and the old tool 'could run forever' with no answer and no signal that it had given up.
brief.how_it_works: An A* search tries chains of decoders, running fast ones like Base64 first and ordering the rest with a heuristic from the cipher_identifier crate. Candidate outputs are checked for plaintext by an English checker (trigram and dictionary based), LemmeKnow (a Rust port of pyWhat that recognises more than 120 formats), and a common-password check, and the search stops at the first candidate that passes. Decoders run in parallel with Rayon, and results are cached in ~/.ciphey/database.sqlite.

brief.install_notes: cargo install ciphey is the main route. Prebuilt binaries for Linux x86_64, macOS (Intel and Apple silicon), and Windows x86_64 are on the GitHub releases page, each with a .sha256 checksum. Building from source needs a Rust toolchain. On first run, a short setup asks for a colour theme, how results are shown, and whether to use a wordlist, then writes ~/.ciphey/config.toml. The Ares-era README also mentions a BERT-based 'enhanced detection' option that needs a one-time download of a roughly 500MB model and a free Hugging Face account, enabled with 'ciphey --enable-enhanced-detection'; the current README does not mention it. A Dockerfile exists per the older README (git clone, then docker build .). The brew formula gives no extra install steps.
brief.standout: Most decoders need you to name the cipher, or they brute-force one at a time. This tool searches chains of decoders with no key or hint, and its crib mode (-r with a regex like flag\{) suits CTF work. It also reports what the plaintext is (for example an IP address, a TOTP URI, or a password in a mount command), not just the decoded string.
brief.status: Unknown as to exact dates: neither page shows a last-commit or release date. Evidence of ongoing work: the current README mentions an MCP server and a crates.io 0.12.0 release that is behind master, plus a Notion doc and a Discord bot. The Ares-named page carries an older README (Dec 2022 screenshot, 16 decoders), so the two pages are at different points in the project's history.
brief.caveats: Name mismatch: the brew formula is named 'ares' with executable 'ares', but the README describes the 'ciphey' crate and binary, and says Ares was the old name. Check the binary name after install. The bee-san/Ares URL serves an older README for the same project, and the current README lives at bee-san/Ciphey. Plaintext detection is imperfect: very short phrases, non-English text, JSON, and unusual flag formats can be missed or misidentified. The default timeout is 5 seconds. The library API on master differs from the crates.io 0.12.0 release (a git dependency is needed for the newer functions). The MCP feature is not in a crates.io release yet. Licence is MIT. The homepage fetch did not fail, but the content may not match what the brew formula's description implies. The decoder count differs between sources: 16 in the Ares-era README, 24 in the current one.
quotes: ciphey is the next generation of decoding tools, built by the same people that brought you Ciphey.
Paste in text that's been encoded or encrypted. Ciphey works out how and hands you the plaintext.
No key, no cipher name, no hints.
One of the big issues with Ciphey is that it could run forever. If it couldn't decode your text, you'd never know!
